Chemistry of Cast Iron Seasoning: A Science-Based How-To

Flaxseed oil sucks for seasoning.

We have a couple dozen cast iron pans, and I've stripped and reseasoned every one of them.

Canola oil is my preferred goto, but regular crisco works well, too.

People try flaxseed and olive oil because they give a darker color quickly and it makes the pans pretty.

However - flaxseed oil has much much higher cohesive vs adhesive properties than other oils, which is why it flakes off for so many who use it. It sticks to itself better than it sticks to the pan (especially if you have a sanded-smooth cooking surface.) It looks good right away, but one acidic dish is enough to start it peeling and flaking.

This lady's methods aren't too bad, but her obsession with making shiny pans is misguided.

If you want a shiny black pan to display, then just buy a can of krypton.

If you want a good workhorse, then use cheap oil, and just keep cooking with it.

My personal recommendations:

  1. Strip everything down to bare metal. Easy-off in a trash bag for 3-5 days is good, I've also used an electrolysis tank of sorts. Easy off is easier, but not nearly as fun.

  2. Wire brush and hot soapy water to get it down to bare metal.

  3. Soak in a strong vinegar mixture for about a half hour to neutralize any remaining easy off, and also to strip the last layer of oxide from the iron.

  4. From this point on, use a lint-free cloth. Little hairs in your seasoning suck.

  5. Rinse with hit running water, and dry the pan as well as possible, and put into a 175°F oven for about 30 minutes to thoroughly dry. Iron is porous to some degree, the oven helps dry it better than just a cloth can. Too hot can cause issues when the oil is added.

  6. There will be orange oxide forming on the pan. Bare iron + oxygen = oxide. (Technically "rust" and "oxide" refer to the same process and can be used interchangeably.) You can't avoid this. If you add anything after the vinegar and rinse that "helps prevent flash rust" the you are adding some barrier to the bare iron. Don't. The seasoning is the barrier you want, and it won't adhere to the iron if something else is already there.

  7. For the very first layer of seasoning only: Pour a crapload of oil into the pan. Seriously, like a half cup. Swirl it around, wipe it everywhere, really let it saturate every surface. This step is to make certain there is no exposed bare metal. (For all other layers, only use a puddle about the size of a quarter, and wipe down the whole pan with it. A little will go a long way.) The first layer will likely leave the rag a little orange, that is fine.

  8. For every layer of seasoning: wipe off as much oil as you can with a clean lint free cloth. Really try to wipe it all off. This will leave a very thin layer (.0002-.0004") of oil, which is exactly what is needed.

  9. Look online to find the 'smoke point' of the oil you are using. Add 20% to that number, and set the stove to that temperature. (Doesn't have to be exact.)

  10. Put the pan in the oven upside down - to prevent any pooling of any oil that may seep out.

  11. Let the pan warm up with the oven. Don't put the (empty) pan in a 450+ oven, it could possibly lead to warping..

  12. I keep it at temperature for 2 hours, other people have good luck with as little as 1 hour. Regardless, after 2 hours, turn off the oven and let it cool down naturally- again, rapid temperature change with an empty pan can lead to warping.

  13. Repeat steps 7-12 until you have at least 3 layers of seasoning.

  14. Now cook with your pan. It is a pan, not a display piece. Cook with it. Make bacon in it, cornbread, steaks, whatever. The more often you use it, the better it will look.

  15. Do not cook anything acidic in it for a few months - tomato sauce, wine, lemon, vinegar etc can eat away a little seasoning so it is better to wait until it is well-used.

  16. CLEANING WITH SOAPY WATER IS FINE! Great-grandma's soap had lye in it. That is bad. Today's soap has perfume in it instead. It won't hurt the seasoning.

  17. Stuck-on food comes off easiest if you just put water in the pan, bring to a boil to soften the food, then wipe out the ick. Chain mail is overrated.

  18. Get and use a square-ended metal spatula. Repeatedly scraping it across the cook surface will help make it smoother over time.

  19. There is nothing wrong with occasionally adding another seasoning layer, I'll add a few of mine to the oven whenever I add a newcomer to my collection.

  20. Keep cooking with it.
